title: Pancytopenia
subject: Medicine
summary: Pancytopenia is a simultaneous reduction of red cells, white cells and platelets. It signals bone‑marrow failure or peripheral destruction and demands a focused, stepwise work‑up, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Pancytopenia is defined when haemoglobin <10 g/dL, absolute neutrophil count <1.5 ×10⁹/L and platelet count <100 ×10⁹/L on two separate samples taken 24 h apart.
b: Requires a peripheral blood film to look for dysplasia, blasts or parasites
Bone‑marrow aspiration/biopsy is the definitive test to differentiate production failure from peripheral loss

sections.p: Severity is graded by the lowest line count; severe disease is any count below the thresholds above, especially ANC <0.5 ×10⁹/L (high infection risk).
b: Mild: all counts just below normal limits
Moderate: at least one line <50 % of lower reference
Severe: ANC <0.5 ×10⁹/L or platelets <20 ×10⁹/L

sections.p: In East African hospitals the commonest aetiologies are infections and marrow‑infiltrative disorders.
b: HIV infection – marrow suppression, opportunistic infections
Visceral leishmaniasis (kala‑azar) – massive splenomegaly, LD bodies in marrow
Tuberculosis – granulomatous marrow infiltration
Aplastic anaemia – idiopathic or benzene/radiation exposure
Malaria (severe) – hemolysis plus marrow suppression
Drug‑induced (e.g., chloramphenicol, anti‑TB drugs)
Nutritional deficiencies (vitamin B12, folate) – megaloblastic marrow

sections.p: Patients usually present with fatigue, easy bruising or bleeding, recurrent infections and, when splenomegaly is present, abdominal fullness.
b: Pallor and tachycardia from anaemia
Petechiae, gum bleeding or menorrhagia from thrombocytopenia
Fever, oral ulcers, or skin pustules from neutropenia
Massive, non‑tender splenomegaly suggests leishmaniasis or TB

t.b: Confirms pancytopenia and quantifies severity; guides urgency of antimicrobial prophylaxis
Looks for parasites (malaria, leishmania), dysplasia, blasts; if unavailable, rely on clinical clues and treat presumptively
Identifies a common reversible cause; positive test prompts CD4 count and opportunistic infection screen

t.a: Serology for Leishmania (rK39) or bone‑marrow aspirate if feasible
t.b: Detects LD bodies; if marrow not available, treat empirically in endemic area with splenomegaly

t.a: Chest X‑ray and sputum for TB (if cough or weight loss)
t.b: Detects pulmonary TB that may also involve marrow
Distinguishes aplastic marrow (hypocellular) from infiltrative disease; essential when infection screens are negative
Identifies reversible megaloblastic pancytopenia; treat with vitamins if low

sections.p: Severe neutropenia and thrombocytopenia can rapidly lead to life‑threatening infection or hemorrhage.
b: Fever >38 °C with ANC <0.5 ×10⁹/L – start broad‑spectrum antibiotics
Uncontrolled bleeding or platelet count <20 ×10⁹/L – consider platelet transfusion if available
Signs of high‑output cardiac failure in severe anaemia

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; provide supportive care while awaiting definitive diagnosis.
b: Empiric antileishmanial therapy (e.g., sodium stibogluconate) in endemic area with splenomegaly when marrow unavailable
Start antiretroviral therapy after HIV diagnosis; screen for opportunistic infections
If aplastic anaemia suspected and no transplant option, give oral cyclosporine (avoid ATG if unavailable) and transfuse as needed
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) for febrile neutropenia; avoid aminoglycosides if renal function unknown
Transfuse packed red cells for Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic anaemia; platelet transfusion only for active bleeding or <20 ×10⁹/L

sections.p: Monitor counts weekly until stable; address preventable causes.
b: Repeat CBC after 2 weeks of therapy to assess response
Vaccinate against encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, Hib) once neutrophil recovery begins
Educate on avoiding marrow toxins (benzene, unregulated herbal remedies)
Provide insect‑net use and prompt malaria treatment to reduce secondary marrow suppression
Aplastic anaemia – similar labs but marrow is empty; no splenomegaly
Myelodysplastic syndrome – dysplastic cells and often older patients; blasts may be present
Severe malaria – may cause anaemia and thrombocytopenia but usually not neutropenia
Peripheral smear may appear normal in early leishmaniasis; rely on clinical picture
HIV rapid test can be false‑negative in early infection; repeat if suspicion high
Bone‑marrow cellularity can be patchy; a single aspirate may miss focal infiltrates

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in haemoglobin causing chest pain or syncope

faq.q: Why is a bone‑marrow biopsy essential?
faq.a: It tells whether the problem is production failure (hypocellular marrow) or peripheral destruction/infiltration, directing therapy.
Severe malaria can depress all lines, but neutropenia is less common; persistent pancytopenia after parasite clearance suggests another cause.

faq.q: What is the first step in a febrile patient with pancytopenia?
faq.a: Start broad‑spectrum antibiotics promptly while arranging cultures and assessing ANC.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer from rural Kenya presents with fever, massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia. What is your most likely diagnosis and why? — Look for visceral leishmaniasis; splenomegaly, endemic area, LD bodies on marrow.

You receive a CBC showing Hb 8 g/dL, ANC 0.4 ×10⁹/L, platelets 15 ×10⁹/L. What immediate management steps do you take? — Start empiric antibiotics, arrange blood/platelet transfusion, and begin work‑up for HIV/TB/leishmania.

How does aplastic anaemia differ from peripheral destruction on marrow examination? — Aplastic shows a hypocellular, fatty marrow; peripheral destruction shows a normocellular or hypercellular marrow with infiltrates.
Why is a peripheral smear insufficient to rule out leishmaniasis in a patient with pancytopenia? — Parasites may be absent from blood; marrow or splenic aspirate is needed for definitive diagnosis.

A patient on long‑term chloramphenicol develops pancytopenia. What is the mechanism and what should you do? — Drug‑induced marrow suppression; stop chloramphenicol and provide supportive transfusions.

What vaccinations are indicated once neutrophil recovery begins in a pancytopenic patient? — Pneumococcal, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and influenza vaccines to prevent encapsulated bacterial infections.
Explain why platelet transfusion is not given routinely to all pancytopenic patients. — Risks of alloimmunisation and limited resources; reserved for active bleeding or very low counts.

In a resource‑limited setting without bone‑marrow facilities, how would you prioritize investigations for pancytopenia? — CBC, peripheral smear, HIV test, malaria smear, rK39 rapid test, and chest X‑ray; treat presumptively based on most likely endemic cause.
